text: The claim log and the predicate are read by different consumers and must be able to move independently; coupling them means an unrelated format revs whenever the other does

Considered deriving the version inside attest from a package-level var rather than passing it in; rejected because two sources for one version is two things that can disagree, and the one in a signed trail is the one nobody can correct afterwards

Hashing os.Executable() at run time describes the binary that actually produced the statement, which a build-time constant could not; the failure paths return empty so the digest is omitted rather than faked

Could not establish whether the digest failure path (unreadable or deleted executable) behaves correctly in a real deployment; the test exercises the omission via an empty Digest rather than by making os.Executable fail

The four-value taxonomy conflated two orthogonal axes — whether clearing was correct, and who was at fault when it was not — which is why immaterial and irrelevant felt suspicious; irrelevant is a pawl defect report, not a judgement about a claim

Considered collapsing immaterial and irrelevant into one value as the spec suggested; rejected because they attribute to different owners — an incomplete claim is an agent failure, a mis-anchored claim is a bug in pawl — and averaging them into one rate makes the number unactionable

Splitting the axes largely removes the retrofit risk the spec was blocked on: axis 1 is binary and cannot be invalidated by later refinement, so only the cause enum grows and previously recorded false-clear rates stay comparable

Could not establish how often reviewers will disagree on claim_incomplete, which requires a subjective judgement about what mattered in a span; recorded as a non-functional concern with double-sampling proposed rather than solved
The real objection to enforced claiming is noise, not latency: not every changed line carries an assumption, so the unit of obligation has to be accounting rather than claiming

Considered the spec's own guess, a trivial claim kind that auto-clears; rejected because trivial claims would land in the claim corpus and the attestation as claims, inflating a count shown to clients
The acknowledgement escape hatch is safe because PAWL-007 samples acknowledged spans, so over-acknowledgement surfaces as a rising false-clear rate rather than being prohibited by rule

Could not establish whether decision-triggered capture of rejected alternatives is achievable at any useful rate; PAWL-015 AC2 and AC5 specify the measurement precisely because the mechanism may turn out not to work
An acknowledgement is given no text field at all, so AC3's no-prose requirement is enforced by the type rather than by convention — there is nowhere for an agent to put prose even if it wanted to

Considered a discriminated union in claims.jsonl rather than a second file; rejected because a separate file makes AC2 structural — nothing reading the claim log can encounter an acknowledgement, so no future code path can start counting one as a claim
A claim outranks an acknowledgement in both directions: a clearing claim still reads clear because it is evidenced rather than waved through, and a claim needing a human still wins under C-8
The ratio divides by accounted lines rather than changed lines so it measures claiming quality rather than how much unclaimed code happened to be in the diff

The hook informs rather than enforces: enforcement already exists at the gate, and what only a hook can supply is the span at the moment of the edit, which is what keeps the answer evidence rather than reconstruction under C-2

Considered having the hook compute changed line ranges itself from the tool payload; rejected because every harness would then reimplement diffing in shell, which is how a thin plugin turns into the harness the build/buy position forbids

git diff HEAD omits untracked files, so a newly created file would report nothing pending and never be accounted for; listing them separately avoids mutating the index, which matters for something running on every edit

Could not establish whether the injected context is the right size or tone in practice; capped at six ranges as a guess, and the acknowledgement ratio plus the unclaimed rate are the signals that will say whether agents act on it or learn to ignore it

A rule may record that there was nothing to assume but may never assert what was assumed, because it does not know; acknowledgement is automatable precisely because it asserts nothing, which is the boundary the whole spec turns on

Considered a self-reported token count as the cost measure; kept it but demoted it to provenance beside ts and harness, because the verifiable proxy — the share of records pawl produced by rule — needs nobody's word for it
Cost must never reach the gate: the moment a verdict depends on it, an agent is paid to claim less, and under-claiming is the failure the tool exists to catch

Could not establish what share of a real session's acknowledgements are actually rule-decidable; the estimate that auto-ack removes roughly half the token cost reasons from one session's shape rather than measurement

Eager surfacing produces worse records, not just costlier ones: a claim recorded while its span is still being edited will not match by the time work settles, so claiming early manufactures the drift that C-4 exists to report
The cache must never influence a verdict; if it did, a machine-local file nobody reviews would decide what merges, and deleting it would change the gate outcome

Considered ignoring .pawl/ entirely to keep the trail out of the diff; that was already wrong and is now reverted — DefaultExcludes handles the counting problem, and ignoring the directory meant CI would read no records at all

Could not establish whether deferring to turn end is late enough to let spans settle in practice, or whether agents will simply not respond once the edit is no longer immediate; the ratio and unclaimed rate are the signals that will say
